1.1.audience: A mathematics undergraduate who knows basic probability and calculus but may never have seen filtrations, martingales, stochastic integrals, or Lean.
1.1.question: How can we do calculus when the path itself is random?
1.1.promise: By the end, you should be able to explain why Brownian motion is the noise source, why the integrand must use only past information, how the Itô integral is built from finite sums, why stopping rescues locally square-integrable integrands, and what Itô's formula contributes to SDEs.
before_you_start: You need ordinary expectation and variance, basic real analysis, and the idea of an integral.
You do not need measure-theoretic probability fluency yet. Whenever a sigma-algebra or almost-everywhere statement becomes essential, Samplinglib explains why it is needed.
You do not need Lean. The green Lean layer stays closed until you choose Lean learner mode.

story.title: 1. A Brownian motion is a random continuous path
story.intuition: Imagine drawing a new continuous, extremely jagged curve every time the experiment runs. At a fixed time \(t\), \(B_t\) is a random variable; as \(t\) varies, the whole family is a stochastic process.
story.tiny_example: The increment \(B_{t+h}-B_t\) has mean \(0\) and variance \(h\). So a time interval four times as long produces twice the typical displacement, because standard deviation scales like \(\sqrt h\).
story.remember: Brownian motion is continuous in time but not differentiable in the ordinary calculus sense. That is why ordinary chain rule must be replaced later by Itô's formula.

story.title: 2. A filtration records what information is available by time \(t\)
story.intuition: A filtration \(\mathcal F_t\) is a growing collection of observable events. If \(s\le t\), anything known at time \(s\) is still known at time \(t\).
story.tiny_example: If you have watched the Brownian path up to 10 seconds, you know everything you knew at 5 seconds, but not the future increment from 10 to 11 seconds.
story.remember: Adapted means 'no peeking into the future'. This is the information-theoretic reason the coefficient multiplying the next Brownian increment must be measurable using current information.

story.title: 3. Build the Itô integral first for stepwise adapted processes
story.intuition: Before integrating a complicated random process \(\eta_t\), freeze it on each time cell. The stochastic integral is then just a finite sum: current coefficient times the next Brownian increment.
story.tiny_example: On two cells, the integral looks like \(H_0(B_{t_1}-B_{t_0})+H_1(B_{t_2}-B_{t_1})\), where \(H_0\) is known at \(t_0\) and \(H_1\) is known at \(t_1\).
story.remember: The first construction is finite-dimensional algebra. The analytic difficulty enters only when we pass to limits.

story.title: 4. The Itô isometry turns stochastic integration into an \(L^2\) geometry problem
story.intuition: Independent mean-zero Brownian increments make the cross terms disappear. The expected square of the stochastic integral therefore equals the expected time integral of \(\eta_t^2\).
story.tiny_example: For a deterministic constant \(c\) on \([0,T]\), \(\mathbb E[(\int_0^T c\,dB_t)^2]=c^2T=\int_0^T c^2\,dt\).
story.remember: This identity is the bridge that lets us complete elementary integrands in \(L^2\) instead of defining the general Itô integral path-by-path.

story.title: 5. \(L^2\) completion defines the integral for general square-integrable integrands
story.intuition: Approximate \(\eta\) by elementary processes \(\eta^n\). If \(\eta^n\) is Cauchy in the process \(L^2\) norm, the Itô isometry says their terminal stochastic integrals are Cauchy in \(L^2(\Omega)\), so a unique limit exists.
story.tiny_example: This is the same completion idea used to construct \(L^2\) functions from simple functions: define the difficult object as the unique limit of easy objects under a norm that controls exactly what matters.
story.remember: At this point the integral is an \(L^2\) equivalence class. Getting one continuous process for all times requires another argument, such as Doob maximal control plus a pathwise limiting construction.

story.title: 6. Stopping and localization let us integrate processes that are only locally square-integrable
story.intuition: A path may accumulate too much total energy globally. Stop it when its accumulated energy reaches level \(n+1\). Before that random time, the stopped integrand has a deterministic \(L^2\) energy bound.
story.tiny_example: Think of a machine that is safe while cumulative heat stays below \(n+1\). The stopping time is the first moment the heat meter reaches the threshold; after that we turn the machine off.
story.remember: The hard point is not the slogan 'stop at high energy'. One must prove the hitting time is a stopping time, the stopped integrand stays measurable/progressive, its \(L^2\) energy is finite, and stochastic integrals agree on overlapping stopping horizons.

story.title: 7. Itô's formula is the chain rule adapted to quadratic variation
story.intuition: Brownian increments are of order \(\sqrt{dt}\), so their squares are of order \(dt\) and survive in the limit. This creates the second-derivative correction absent from ordinary calculus.
story.tiny_example: For \(f(x)=x^2\), Itô's formula gives \(d(B_t^2)=2B_t\,dB_t+dt\). The extra \(dt\) term records accumulated quadratic variation.
story.remember: The correction is not a mysterious convention: it is the limiting contribution of squared Brownian increments.

story.title: 8. An SDE combines deterministic drift with stochastic forcing
story.intuition: Once stochastic integration and Itô calculus are available, an equation \(dX_t=b(X_t)\,dt+\sigma(X_t)\,dB_t\) can be read as an integral equation and studied for existence, uniqueness, and dynamics.
story.tiny_example: The Langevin SDE later uses a drift pushing toward high target density and Brownian noise that keeps the process exploring.
story.remember: Chapter 1.2 will stop looking at one path construction and start studying the evolution through transition kernels, semigroups, generators, and invariant laws.

vocabulary: A time-indexed family of random variables; equivalently, a random path when viewed sample by sample.
The information available up to time \(t\). It grows with time.
At time \(t\), the process value can be determined from \(\mathcal F_t\); it does not use future information.
A fair-game process: conditional on current information, the expected future value equals the present value.
A joint time-sample measurability condition strong enough to support stopping and stochastic integration.
A random time \(\tau\) for which deciding whether \(\tau\le t\) requires only information available by \(t\).
A process that becomes a genuine martingale after stopping along an increasing localizing sequence.
Finite second-moment geometry. Norm convergence in \(L^2\) is the completion mechanism behind the Itô integral.
Statements allowed to fail on a set of measure/probability zero. Lean forces the relevant measure to be explicit.
The accumulated squared-increment effect that survives for Brownian paths and produces the Itô correction.

1.2.audience: A mathematics undergraduate who has just learned what an SDE is and now wants to understand long-time behavior without following every sample path.
1.2.question: How do we study a diffusion through operators instead of individual noisy trajectories?
1.2.promise: You will connect transition probabilities to a Markov semigroup, differentiate the semigroup to obtain a generator, then see how stationarity, reversibility, Dirichlet forms, Poincaré/LSI, and Bakry–Émery turn local differential structure into global convergence rates.
before_you_start: Know conditional expectation at an intuitive level.
Remember that Chapter 1.1 constructs stochastic paths; this section packages their law-level evolution.
story: 1. Transition kernel
For each starting point \(x\) and elapsed time \(t\), record the probability law of where the process lands.
2. Markov semigroup \(P_t\)
Apply the transition law to a test function \(f\). The value \(P_t f(x)\) is the expected future value of \(f\) when starting from \(x\).
3. Generator \(L\)
Differentiate \(P_t\) at \(t=0\). The generator \(L\) is the infinitesimal velocity of observables and, for Langevin, becomes a differential operator.
4. Stationarity and reversibility
Ask which probability law is unchanged by \(P_t\), then whether time evolution is symmetric in \(L^2\) of that law.
5. Carré du champ and Dirichlet energy
Use \(L\) to measure how strongly a function varies. This turns probabilistic mixing into an energy estimate.
6. Poincaré and log-Sobolev
Functional inequalities say variance or entropy is controlled by the corresponding energy. Dissipation then becomes exponential decay.
7. Bakry–Émery
Differentiate the energy again. Curvature lower bounds on \(\Gamma_2\) provide a structural route to functional inequalities.
vocabulary: The derivative of the semigroup at time zero on its domain.
A distribution \(\pi\) satisfying \(\pi P_t=\pi\) for every \(t\).
The semigroup is self-adjoint in \(L^2(\pi)\), a detailed-balance symmetry.
Variance is bounded by a constant times Dirichlet energy.
Entropy is bounded by a constant times Fisher/Dirichlet-type information.

1.3.audience: A mathematics undergraduate comfortable with metric spaces and probability measures but new to optimal transport.
1.3.question: How can distance between probability distributions itself become a geometry?
1.3.promise: You will start with couplings, build quadratic transport cost and \(W_2\), then understand optimal plans, duality, gluing, geodesics, continuity equations, and dynamic transport.
before_you_start: Know what a probability measure and expectation are.
A little metric-space intuition is enough; the measure-theoretic details can be unfolded when needed.
story: 1. Coupling
Put two distributions on one joint probability space while preserving each marginal.
2. Transport cost
A coupling tells us how much mass moves from \(x\) to \(y\); integrate a cost such as \(\lVert x-y\rVert^2\).
3. Wasserstein distance
Choose the cheapest coupling and take the square root of the quadratic cost.
4. Duality and optimal maps
Replace a minimization over joint measures by potentials; under regularity, optimal transport can be represented by a map.
5. Gluing and the metric property
Glue couplings through a common marginal; this is the probabilistic engine behind the triangle inequality.
6. Curves and continuity equations
A moving probability law can be described by a velocity field transporting mass.
7. Benamou–Brenier and geodesics
The distance \(W_2\) can be recovered as the least kinetic action, and optimal transport plans generate constant-speed geodesics.
vocabulary: A joint law with prescribed first and second marginals.
Another name for a coupling when interpreted as moving mass.
The quadratic Wasserstein distance obtained from optimal expected squared displacement.
A coupling attaining the transport infimum.
A PDE expressing conservation of probability mass under a velocity field.
The curve of measures obtained by moving particles along optimal straight paths.

1.4.audience: A mathematics undergraduate who has seen gradients in Euclidean optimization and has just learned \(W_2\) geometry.
1.4.question: In what precise sense is Langevin diffusion gradient descent on probability distributions?
1.4.promise: You will translate Euclidean gradient-flow ideas into Wasserstein space: first variation, KL functional, Fokker–Planck equation, geodesic convexity, energy dissipation, contraction, and functional inequalities.
before_you_start: Recall ordinary gradient flow \(\dot x=-\nabla F(x)\).
Know the basic \(W_2\) geodesic picture from Section 1.3.
story: 1. Functional instead of function
The optimization variable is now a probability distribution \(\rho\), and the objective is a functional such as \(\mathrm{KL}(\rho\,\|\,\pi)\).
2. First variation
Ask how the functional changes under an infinitesimal movement of mass.
3. Wasserstein gradient
Use the \(W_2\) metric structure to convert that first variation into a velocity field.
4. Fokker–Planck equals \(\mathrm{KL}\) gradient flow
The law of Langevin diffusion satisfies the same PDE generated by descending \(\mathrm{KL}\) in Wasserstein geometry.
5. Geodesic convexity
Convexity along \(W_2\) geodesics plays the role of ordinary convexity along straight lines.
6. Dissipation and contraction
Gradient-flow identities convert convexity or functional inequalities into decay of \(\mathrm{KL}\) and contraction in \(W_2\).
7. Talagrand / PL viewpoints
Different inequalities compare function value, gradient size, and distance to equilibrium, mirroring optimization theory.
vocabulary: A function whose input is itself a function or probability measure.
The measure-space analogue of a directional derivative.
Steepest descent of a functional measured in \(W_2\) geometry.
The PDE describing how the probability density of an SDE evolves.
Convexity tested along geodesics of the probability metric space.
An identity or inequality showing the objective decreases according to a squared gradient/information quantity.

1.5.audience: A mathematics undergraduate who wants a map of the convergence guarantees before entering later technical chapters.
1.5.question: Once we know the diffusion converges, which distance should we measure and how does initialization enter?
1.5.promise: You will compare \(\mathrm{TV}\), \(\mathrm{KL}\), \(\chi^2\), and \(W_2\), see how divergence inequalities transfer bounds, and understand why warm starts and initialization estimates matter in sampling complexity.
before_you_start: Know that different probability distances emphasize different kinds of error.
Remember the Poincaré/LSI decay routes and \(W_2\) contraction routes from Sections 1.2–1.4.
story: 1. Several notions of error
\(\mathrm{TV}\) controls event probabilities, \(\mathrm{KL}\) measures relative information, \(\chi^2\) is a stronger density-ratio error, and \(W_2\) measures geometric displacement.
2. Comparison inequalities
A bound in a strong divergence can imply a bound in a weaker metric, but constants and assumptions matter.
3. Initialization
Continuous-time contraction only helps after we quantify how far the initial law is from the target.
4. Data processing
Passing distributions through the same Markov kernel cannot increase an \(f\)-divergence.
5. Variational and chain-rule tools
Donsker–Varadhan and \(\mathrm{KL}\) chain rules let us decompose or optimize information-theoretic quantities.
6. Convergence overview
The chapter closes by matching structural assumptions to a metric, a dissipation/contraction mechanism, and an initialization bound.
vocabulary: The largest discrepancy in probability assigned to the same measurable event.
Expected log density ratio; asymmetric and information-theoretic.
Expected squared density-ratio deviation; often stronger than \(\mathrm{KL}\).
A common stochastic transformation cannot increase an \(f\)-divergence.
An initial law already controlled relative to the target, making later mixing estimates effective.
A variational characterization of \(\mathrm{KL}\) using exponential moments of test functions.
